target.title: Brain-to-text: decoding spoken phrases from phone representations in the brain

read.pdf: Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–2 read from the text extraction

entries.text: The authors claim the first decoding of continuously spoken speech into expressed words from intracranial ECoG.
entries.condition: Overt continuous speech; intracranial electrocorticographic recordings; decoded output is expressed words.

entries.text: The study recorded seven epilepsy patients with clinically implanted ECoG grids.
entries.condition: Patients at Albany Medical Center; grids implanted for presurgical epilepsy care; all had left-hemisphere electrodes.

entries.text: Participants read prompted English text aloud while ECoG and synchronized acoustic audio were recorded.
entries.condition: Overt read-aloud production, not imagined speech; prompts included historical speeches, a children's story, or fan fiction.
entries.quote: Each subject was instructed to read the text aloud as it appeared on the screen.

entries.text: Recording sessions contained 21–49 phrases and lasted 126.37–590.10 seconds in Table 1; the paper reports sessions repeated 2–3 times depending on participant condition.
entries.unit: phrases per session; seconds per session
entries.condition: Across the Table 1 sessions for seven participants; texts were segmented at pauses; participant 6 has one listed session.

entries.text: Both sessions for participant 4 and session 2 for participant 5 were excluded after the speech-activity preselection failed to distinguish speech-related activation from chance.
entries.condition: Participant 4: both sessions; participant 5: session 2; rejection followed a t-test with p > 0.05.
entries.quote: both sessions of subject 4 and session 2 of subject 5 were rejected

entries.text: Audio transcripts were force-aligned by an English broadcast-news ASR model, then aligned again after session-specific acoustic-model adaptation; the resulting phone labels served as neural labels.
entries.condition: Viterbi forced alignment conditioned on the known text; session-dependent MLLR adaptation used high-confidence segments; labels were imposed on synchronized ECoG.
entries.quote:
Phone labels of the acoustic recordings were created in a three-
step process using an English automatic speech recognition
(ASR) system trained on broadcast news.

entries.text: Acoustic models were adapted separately for each session with MLLR before final forced alignment.
entries.condition: MLLR transformation estimated using the first phone sequence and only segments with high confidence; adaptation was per recording session.

entries.text: The ECoG label inventory grouped similar English phones into reduced phone classes because the neural training set was small.
entries.condition: Phone groupings based on phonetic features; the best-session accuracy statement refers to 20 phones plus SILENCE.
entries.quote: we reduced the amount of distinct phone types and grouped similar phones together for the ECoG models.

entries.text: Features were log broadband-gamma power from 50-ms windows, updated every 25 ms, after channel cleaning and common-average referencing.
entries.unit: ms window; ms overlap/step; Hz broadband gamma
entries.condition: Continuous ECoG; broadband gamma band 70–170 Hz; raw signals detrended, downsampled from 9600 to 600 Hz, noisy channels removed, CAR applied, then log energy computed.
entries.quote: We segmented the neural signal data continuously into 50 ms intervals with an overlap of 25 ms

entries.text: Each feature vector included four preceding and four following feature vectors, yielding a 450-ms phone context.
entries.condition: Stacked feature vectors used for phone classification; surrounding context is present in both past and future.

entries.text: An average of 7.0 channels per subject were removed by the line-noise channel rejection rule (SD 6.5).
entries.condition: Channels whose 58–62-Hz energy exceeded two interquartile ranges above the dataset's third quartile were removed.

entries.text: Each grouped phone was modeled as a multivariate Gaussian with diagonal variance, using one context-independent model per phone.
entries.condition: Means and diagonal variances estimated from training data; no preceding- or succeeding-phone context in the phone model.
entries.quote: only one context-independent model is trained for each phone

entries.text: Feature selection by mean pairwise phone-model KL divergence and LDA dimensionality reduction were performed using training data within each validation fold.
entries.condition: Automatic feature count selected at decline threshold t = −0.05; selection and LDA fit used training labels/data only.

entries.text: Word decoding combined ECoG phone-model likelihoods, a pronunciation dictionary, and an n-gram language model, with Viterbi search for the most likely word sequence.
entries.condition: Phone sequences composed into dictionary words; language prior combined with the neural likelihood; the shown language model is a bigram.
entries.quote: the Viterbi algorithm calculates the most likely word sequence and corresponding phone sequence.

entries.text: Bigram probabilities were estimated on the texts read by the participants, and the same language models were used for neural and randomized-phone analyses.
entries.condition: The text corpus is the prompted reading material; whether the held-out phrase was removed from LM estimation is not stated (see t41).
entries.quote:
For the Brain-to-Text system, we estimate bi-
grams on the texts read by the subjects.

entries.text: For each test phrase, the dictionary included the words actually spoken plus randomized words; the same dictionaries and restricted language models were used for the neural and randomized systems.
entries.condition: Dictionary size varied; target-phrase words were known and guaranteed to be present in the test dictionary.
entries.quote: For this purpose, we created new dictionaries for every test phrase including the words that were actually spoken plus a set of randomized set of words from the full dictionary.

entries.text: Evaluation held out one phrase at a time within a recording session and repeated this for every phrase; all model fitting and feature selection used the remaining phrases.
entries.condition: Within-session, within-participant validation; test and training phrases therefore come from the same speaker/session, with no cross-speaker or cross-session generalization test reported.
entries.quote: we trained neural phone models using all but one phrase of a recording session and decoded the remaining phrase.

entries.text: The reference phone sequence was produced by forced alignment of synchronized speech audio to the prompted text, rather than by independent manual phone transcription.
entries.condition: Acoustic labels obtained using broadcast-news ASR, session-adapted MLLR acoustic models, and a second Viterbi forced alignment.
entries.quote: The phone labels calculated on the acoustic data are then imposed on the ECoG data.

entries.text: The empirical chance control shifted training data by half its length while leaving phone labels unchanged; the randomized phone models and main system shared language-model and dictionary information.
entries.condition: Shift point varied by iteration and session; control preserves ECoG feature properties and label priors but breaks feature-label correspondence.
entries.quote:
we shifted the
training data by half its length in each iteration of the leave-one-
phrase-out validation while the corresponding labels remained
unchanged.

entries.text: Authors report WER as low as 25%; the abstract does not identify the contributing speaker, session, dictionary size, or aggregation for this minimum.
entries.condition: Abstract headline; evaluation uses within-session leave-one-phrase-out testing and phrase-specific dictionaries, but the exact condition for this minimum is not identified in the main text.
entries.quote: Our results demonstrate that our system can achieve word error rates as low as 25% and phone error rates below 50%.

entries.text: At dictionary size 10, the authors state that 75% of words were recognized correctly.
entries.condition: Ten-word dictionary; test phrase words were included along with randomized words; leave-one-phrase-out within-session evaluation; the exact session/aggregation is not stated in this result sentence.
entries.quote: With 10 words in the dictionary, 75% of all words are recognized correctly.

entries.text: The abstract reports phone error rates below 50%, but does not state the subject/session, vocabulary, or aggregation condition for this headline.
entries.condition: Abstract-level result; phone decoding was evaluated on held-out phrases within sessions; exact condition for the minimum/error-rate headline is not given.
entries.quote: Our results demonstrate that our system can achieve word error rates as low as 25% and phone error rates below 50%.

entries.text: The best session had average accuracy above 50% across 20 phones plus SILENCE; the main text does not identify which session was best.
entries.condition: Frame-wise phone classification; best session among evaluated sessions; classes are 20 grouped phones plus SILENCE; session identity is unstated.

entries.text: Phone accuracies were significantly higher than randomized models in all sessions at dictionary size 10 (two-sided t-test, p < 0.05).
entries.condition: Single-phone decoding; all evaluated sessions; two-sided t-test; dictionary reduced to 10 words including words under evaluation.

entries.text: WER was significantly lower than randomized-model WER at all tested dictionary sizes (one-sided paired t-test, p < 0.001).
entries.condition: Paired comparison of Brain-to-Text and randomized models across dictionary sizes; one-sided paired t-test; number of pairs/repetitions is not stated.
entries.quote: Signiﬁcance was analyzed using paired t-tests between the Word Error Rates of Brain-To-Text and the randomized models (p < 0.001, one-sided paired t-test).

entries.text: Authors state phone true-positive rates remain relatively stable as dictionary size increases and that the approach scales well.
entries.condition: Increasing, phrase-specific dictionaries; actual target words remain included; performance compared with randomized models.
entries.quote: The approach scales well for increasing dictionary sizes.

entries.text: Nine temporal intervals were plotted, and the plotted KL-divergences exceeded the 99th percentile of randomized phone-alignment values.
entries.unit: temporal intervals; percentile of randomized KL-divergences
entries.condition: Mean pairwise phone-model KL-divergence on co-registered electrodes; participant 4 excluded from joint analysis; randomized alignment shifts data by half its length.

entries.text: High phone-model discriminability appeared in several regions as early as 200 ms before phone production, including Broca's area.
entries.condition: Mean KL-divergence among phone models over the joint registered brain surface; participant 4 excluded.

entries.text: Sensorimotor discriminability increased before production and motor-area discriminability peaked from 0 to 50 ms after phone onset.
entries.condition: Temporal profile of mean KL-divergence between phone models; 50 ms interval corresponds to average phone length according to the authors.

entries.text: The results section says auditory-region discriminability increased until approximately 150 ms after phone production; the Fig. 4 caption describes auditory-region differences at 100 ms after production.
entries.condition: Body text reports a time course; Fig. 4 caption gives a specific STG time point, so the two descriptions differ.

entries.text: Figure 4's caption places auditory-region discriminability in superior temporal gyrus at 100 ms after production, versus approximately 150 ms in the Results prose.
entries.condition: Caption describes the combined electrode montage of all participants except participant 4; this differs from the Results prose's approximate 150-ms timing.

entries.text: The authors claim the continuous-speech timing and locations of single-phone discriminability extend prior state of the art.
entries.condition: Authors compare phone discrimination during continuous overt production with earlier isolated-phoneme or word studies.

entries.text: The authors claim that language information combined with phone models can reconstruct words in unseen utterances from neural signals.
entries.condition: Offline decoding with dictionary and language-model information; here 'unseen' refers to a held-out phrase, not a held-out speaker.
entries.quote: The computational phone models in combination with language information make it possible to reconstruct words in unseen spoken utterances solely based on neural signals (see Supplementary Video).

entries.text: The authors concede that their evaluations were offline, even though they argue the processing is suitable for future online use.
entries.condition: No online evaluation or real-time participant interaction was reported.
entries.quote: Despite the fact that the evaluations in this article have been performed oﬄine

entries.text: The authors say all processing steps are suitable for eventual real-time online application on desktop computers; this is a prospective claim, not a demonstrated result.
entries.condition: Proposed deployment; the reported evaluations were offline and required implanted ECoG grids.
entries.quote: all processing steps of Brain-to-Text and the decoding approach are well suited for eventual real-time online application on desktop computers.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that context-dependent phone models, known to improve recognition, were omitted because the ECoG training set was too small.
entries.condition: One context-independent model per phone; no preceding/succeeding-phone context modeled.
entries.quote: it requires substantially more training data than available in our ECoG setting.

entries.text: The authors note that each participant contributed only several minutes of ECoG, versus traditional acoustic ASR trained on thousands of hours and language models trained on billions of words.
entries.value: several minutes; thousands of hours; billions of words
entries.unit: ECoG per subject; acoustic training; language-model training
entries.condition: The comparison describes the limited training resources available to this system versus traditional ASR.
entries.quote: our data contained only several minutes of ECoG signals for each subject.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that prompted overt speech recordings contain speech-production, motor, auditory, and language-understanding processes together.
entries.condition: Participants read displayed text aloud; this paper did not test imagined speech.

entries.text: The authors concede substantial performance variability across participants, attributing it to task performance and electrode-grid position and density.
entries.condition: Different participants and clinically determined electrode montages; results singled out participants 1, 2, and 7 as promising.

entries.text: No random seed, number of independent randomizations, or repeated training-run count is reported; the paper only says the shift point differed across iterations.
entries.condition: Applies to randomized-phone controls and any stochasticity in dictionary generation or model fitting.

entries.text: Beyond log power and common-average referencing, no per-feature scaling, standardization, or train/test normalization procedure is specified.
entries.condition: Feature selection and LDA are trained within each fold, but the paper does not state a separate feature normalization rule.

entries.text: The paper does not say whether the held-out phrase was excluded when estimating bigrams from the participants' read texts.
entries.condition: Language model estimation corpus is the same prompted reading material from which test phrases are drawn; phrase-specific test dictionaries explicitly include the spoken words.
entries.quote: For the Brain-to-Text system, we estimate bi- grams on the texts read by the subjects.

entries.text: The exact subject/session and aggregation behind the minimum WER and abstract phone-error headline are not identified in the main text.
entries.condition: The main text gives a 10-word dictionary result and identifies subject 7/session 1 for some figure panels, but does not tie those labels to the abstract minima.
entries.quote: Our results demonstrate that our system can achieve word error rates as low as 25% and phone error rates below 50%.

entries.text: No numerical chance-level WER or phone accuracy is stated in the running text; results are described as significantly above randomized controls and Figure 5 plots the comparison.
entries.condition: Chance level is empirically estimated from shifted training data with unchanged labels; plots have no exact plotted values in the text extraction.

entries.text: No cross-speaker or cross-session test is reported; the stated split holds out phrases inside each recording session.
entries.condition: Training and test phrases necessarily share the session participant; no participant-independent evaluation is described.

entries.text: The authors identify overt speech decoding as a necessary first step toward imagined-speech interaction, and propose eventual communication with scalable vocabularies.
entries.condition: Future implication only; the experiments used overt prompted speech, phrase-specific finite dictionaries, and offline evaluation.
entries.quote: Decoding overt speech production is a necessary ﬁrst step toward human-computer interaction through imagined speech processes.

entries.text: The EMG recognizer uses context-independent phoneme acoustic models; the text does not specify whether these are HMMs or GMMs.
entries.value: Context-independent phoneme acoustic models; HMM/GMM type not specified for the EMG recognizer
entries.condition: The HMM-based system described separately is the Broadcast News recognizer used for forced alignment.
entries.quote:
In this paper,
we demonstrate how to train the phoneme-based acoustic mod-
els with carefully designed electromyographic feature extraction
methods.

entries.text: The pronunciation dictionary is not identified; decoding uses a trigram BN language model, with no further LM training-corpus detail stated.
entries.value: Pronunciation dictionary unspecified; trigram BN language model
entries.condition: The paper identifies the LM as BN but does not specify its training-corpus details.
entries.quote:
The trained acoustic model was used together with a trigram BN
language model for decoding.

entries.text: The decoding vocabulary contains 108 words.
entries.condition: Explicitly restricted to words appearing in the test set; it covers all test sentences.
entries.quote:
To cover all the test sentences, the decoding vocabulary contains 108
words in total.

entries.text: The test sentences are excluded from the language-model training data.
entries.condition: The text explicitly says test sentences do not occur in LM training data.
entries.quote:
Also
note that the test sentences do not exist in the language model
training data.

entries.text: Evaluation uses one male speaker in one recording session, with 380 phonetically balanced training utterances and 120 news-article test utterances from separate sentence sets.
entries.condition: Training uses 38 phonetically balanced sentences read in 10 turns; testing uses 12 news-article sentences read in 10 turns.

entries.text: The best reported WER is 32.0% for the best EMG-feature system.
entries.condition: Best EMG-feature system; feature-method comparison in Figure 5 uses a 50-ms delay and the 108-word test-set-restricted vocabulary. The prose does not name the winning feature code.

entries.text: The paper is marked INTERSPEECH 2006 - ICSLP; the printed conference dates are September 17-21.
entries.condition: The imprint gives Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; month September, year 2006.

questions.q: What speech-decoding result does this paper actually demonstrate?
questions.answer: Offline decoding of prompted, overt read-aloud phrases from intracranial ECoG in seven epilepsy patients, with within-session leave-one-phrase-out evaluation. The abstract reports WER as low as 25% and phone error below 50%, but does not identify the exact speaker/session or vocabulary condition for those minima. It is not a demonstration of imagined speech or real-time communication.

questions.q: How should the 25% WER and 75% correct-word figures be qualified?
questions.answer: The paper reports WER as low as 25% in the abstract and 75% of words recognized correctly with a 10-word dictionary. Every test phrase's actual words were included in its dictionary, while the exact subject/session and aggregation for the headline minimum are not stated in the main text.

questions.q: How independent was the test data from training and language-model information?
questions.answer: Neural phone-model fitting and feature selection held out one phrase within a session, so train and test shared the same speaker/session. Bigrams were estimated from the participants' read texts, but the paper does not say that the held-out phrase was excluded; test dictionaries explicitly included the words spoken in each test phrase.

questions.q: Does the study support claims about imagined speech or online deployment?
questions.answer: No direct demonstration: participants read displayed text aloud and all reported evaluations were offline. Imagined-speech communication and real-time desktop use are presented as future possibilities.

questions.q: What data and modeling limitations do the authors concede?
questions.answer: Each participant provided only several minutes of ECoG, preventing context-dependent phone models; performance varied substantially with task performance and electrode position/density. Prompted overt speech also mixes production, motor, auditory, and language processes.

questions.q: (writer, to reader on priors) Do Jou et al. 2006 and Schultz and Wand 2010 use phone models with a dictionary and n-gram LM, what vocabulary, and were test sentences excluded from the LM?
questions.answer: Jou 2006: phoneme-based acoustic models on EMG, trigram BN LM, 108-word decoding vocabulary covering the test sentences, test sentences not in LM training data. Schultz and Wand 2010: 3-state phoneme HMMs, trigram LM trained on Broadcast News, 101-word BASE vocabulary; LM exclusion not stated.

questions.q: (triage) Does the target cite the EMG priors, state significance for all dictionary sizes, and give 100 ms as a peak in Fig. 4?
questions.answer: No EMG recognition paper in the reference list; 'For all dictionary sizes, the performance is significantly better than randomized results' (Sec. 3.2); Fig. 4 caption describes a 100 ms panel, not a peak.
